content: The International Grape Genomics Program (IGGP) is a collaborative initiative aimed at sequencing the genome of the grapevine species Vitis vinifera L. This project involves research centers from multiple countries, including Australia, France, Chile, Germany, Italy, South Africa, Spain, and the United States. The program was established based on the recognition that, despite the economic importance of the Vitis family as a source of fruit, its biological mechanisms remain poorly understood. While centuries of viticulture have led to the development of sophisticated wine-producing practices, the precise ways in which grapevines interact with their environment, respond to abiotic stresses, and combat pests and diseases are not yet fully elucidated. Historically, agricultural advancements in grapevine cultivation have relied on specific genotypes, propagated through vegetative multiplication and controlled growing conditions to enhance quality and yield. Although these methods have improved grape quality, they have also increased production costs and raised concerns about environmental sustainability. The IGGP posits that a deeper understanding of the grapevine's biology, through genome sequencing, could enable targeted improvements in viticulture without the associated economic and environmental burdens. By identifying the roles of individual genes, researchers aim to enhance grape characteristics and quality in a more predictable and efficient manner. As of March 2007, the IGGP had successfully mapped over half of the grapevine genome. During this research, the Cooperative Research Centre for Viticulture (CRCV), based at the CSIRO Plant Industry Horticulture Unit in Adelaide, Australia, made a significant discovery regarding the origin of white grapes. White grapes exist today due to a rare genetic mutation that occurred thousands of years ago. This mutation involved two adjacent regulatory genes, VvMYBA1 and VvMYBA2, in a red grape ancestor. These genes are responsible for controlling the production of anthocyanin, the pigment that gives red grapes their color. The researchers found that in white grape cultivars, the VvMYBA1 gene is not transcribed, meaning it does not activate the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. Additionally, the VvMYBA2 gene in white grapes contains two specific mutations: one causes an amino acid substitution, and the other results in a frameshift mutation. Either of these mutations alone is sufficient to disrupt the gene's ability to activate anthocyanin production, and when both mutations are present, the result is a white grape cultivar. Genetic analyses of the VvMYBA2 gene across 55 white grape cultivars revealed that all of them shared the same double mutation, indicating a single common ancestor for all white grapes. This suggests that without this original parent vine, white grapes would not exist today. Archaeological evidence, such as white wine residues found in ancient Egyptian pottery, suggests that this mutation occurred at least 3,000 years ago. However, without direct comparison to a known ancient white grape genome, it remains possible that the mutation could have arisen more recently. Interestingly, a similar dual mutation was observed in the last decade. Viticulturist Jesús Galilea Esteban, from the Murillo de Río Leza vineyard in Rioja, Spain, identified a white grape mutation in some Tempranillo vines on his estate. After propagating the white vine and confirming that the mutation did not revert, the new varietal was granted preliminary approval for grape status by the Rioja D.O. In 2000, the first hectare of white Tempranillo was planted in the region. Both the white and red Tempranillo vines share identical leaves, clusters, and berry shapes, as well as similar ripening cycles and susceptibility to pests and diseases. The mutation in this case is thought to have been influenced by environmental factors.
